rv.q: Well, it turns out to be a strongly wrought story of considerable moral complexity, one that will hold your attention all the way to the brutal end.
Plays depending on phone conversations with unseen participants are almost always a bad idea, and China Doll is no exception.
But even she can't rescue the farcical, out-of-context ending.
It is hard to imagine a more disorienting show.
Every so often, Mamet gives him a wonderful line that sums up the dark side of humanity.
But even with Al Pacino putting him through his emotional paces, this tarnished titan is going through hell in a vacuum, with no one to play off but unheard voices on the other end of the telephone.
China Doll offers the sad spectacle of two world-class artists turning in their lamest work.
In the meantime, Al Pacino, for whom the role was written, huffs and puffs his way through a performance that remains oddly tentative despite all the showboating mannerisms.
If Pacino had not signed on, would anyone have bothered with this at all?
China Doll, his shaky new Broadway vehicle, by David Mamet, offers flashes of that brilliance between long mucky passages in which he appears to be hunting for the narrative, if not the next line.
Mr. Pacino spends most of the evening pacing and prowling and shouting into a cellphone, like a lion in a very expensive cage.
The evening feels like an ordeal for everyone involved, including the audience.
Whatever Mamet's points, he and Pacino consistently engage us -- which is more than you can say for a lot of the folks the playwright is targeting here.

If CHINA DOLL doesn't set off the sparks of a SPEED-THE-PLOW or an OLEANNA, it does provide enough of the old Mamet tension and cynicism that makes decent people feel disgust for the world we live in.
Much of the language is sublime and there are great one liners along the way.
If China Doll has its weaknesses--and it has--it also has Al Pacino.
“China Doll” is muddled, but it's still a treat to see Pacino, even if we're not always sure what he's doing.
Whatever one thinks of that sort of attitude as policy, as the basis of a drama it's disastrous.
Pacino, looking somewhat frail and moving slowly, delivers his lines in a near-whisper that forces audience members to lean forward and strain to hear him.
Practically a monologue over two hours featuring Pacino mostly conversing on the phone, the script is a rambling mess.

That’s more than can be said for the rest of the play, which, given the price of tickets, resembles for most theatergoers the experience of paying for an internship as Donald Trump’s lackey, forced to witness the conversations of a madman without the luxury of exasperated interruption.
So why bother to write a play for him?
First of all, David Mamet’s script is nearly lifeless.
China Doll is less a play than a very expensive therapy session that we've been forced to attend.
China Doll is an exasperating spectacle of poor writing and dispirited stellar performing that comes close to being an outright debacle.
Despite the play’s problems, Pacino’s theatrics throw it off further dramatically.

“'China Doll' struggles mightily to make sense of byzantine, virtually incomprehensible two-hour monologue; Pam MacKinnon struggles to have Pacino speak like a fast-talking Mamet character, rather than slipping into his idiosyncratic verbal rhythms, and the audience struggles to pay attention --or even stay awake...
This latest work from the one-time master of the blistering, testosterone-fueled style of American drama is simultaneously flabby (meandering monologues) and undeveloped (sketchy storyline).
Pacino fails to make phone calls anything but drudgery.

Posted by: Steve in Broadway, Drama, Featured, Reviews December 9, 2015 0 377 Views By Jennifer Vazquez (@JENerationV) All eyes are transfixed on legendary actor Al Pacino throughout his intense performance in China Doll – the newest creation of Pulitzer Prize playwright David Mamet.

cn.t: Mamet's latest play draws scathing reviews, with critics calling it thin, meandering, and dramatically inert—a disappointing vehicle even for Pacino's star power, which can't salvage what many deem an underdeveloped, tedious two-hour monologue.

sg.ra: Shubert/SeatPlan place rows C-E as 'just right' — close enough to catch facial detail without the stage-height skew that rows AA/A suffer inside this shallow 26'9" proscenium house; TickPick singles out row B (seats 105-110) as the best seat in the Schoenfeld.

SeatPlan notes the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but only begins clipping the top of the stage at row Q — so K-P sits in the narrow band that's still unobstructed yet priced below premium; TickPick and Headout independently flag K-P as the value pocket in this 1,079-seat Shubert house.

sg.vl: Overhang cuts the top of the stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly says rows beyond Q lose the top of the stage to the mezzanine overhang, and Headout/TickPick corroborate that under-overhang seats 'might have obstructed views from the overhang of the box seats or the mezzanine itself' — a real issue in this shallow Shubert house where the mezz projects forward.

sg.vl: Overhead sweep of the whole stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both cite front center mezz rows A-B as offering 'excellent overhead views perfect for appreciating the stage in one sweep' — the Schoenfeld's mezz hangs closer to the stage than larger Shubert houses, so row A feels surprisingly close rather than distant.

SeatPlan flags E-G as benefiting from 'great rake for aerial views which cover the entire stage below' — the Schoenfeld mezz is steeper than most Shubert houses, so E-G keeps the full stage visible where a flatter rake would start clipping; Headout calls it a value tier below the premium A-D band.

Multiple sources describe rear mezz past row F as 'a gamble... actors start to look like LEGO figures' — despite the Schoenfeld only having 392 mezz seats, the steep rake trades sightline for proximity and you lose emotional read on faces; a J104 reviewer conceded 'nearly center, no obstructions' but 2nd-to-last row.

SeatPlan notes 'single-digit seats in rows A-D' of the side mezz 'are more directly above the stage and feel surprisingly close' — the Schoenfeld's narrow 40-foot proscenium means side-mezz angles are less punishing than wider houses, though TickPick warns the far edges of rows 'have slightly blocked views of the corners of the stage'.
